strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: first large-scale long-term RVOS dataset with 2,193 videos averaging 60+ seconds, compared to existing datasets with only 4-13 second clips

Comprehensive and well-curated dataset: 24,689 text descriptions, 2.1M masks, 163 object categories, diverse sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), with rigorous annotation workflow including validation and iterative correction
Well-motivated evaluation metrics: tIoU and vIoU address practical limitations of per-frame metrics by assessing temporal consistency and the ability to predict object absence

Thorough benchmarking demonstrating clear challenges: 6 SOTA methods evaluated consistently; oracle analysis reveals ~25% performance gap (52.8-54.5 vs 77.3-80.6 J&F) demonstrating long-video challenges
Fine-grained evaluation reveals systematic model biases: all methods perform better on static descriptions than dynamic ones, enabling targeted future research
Ablation studies show practical value of motion: +1.6% J&F improvement with just one motion frame, encouraging exploration of motion-enhanced long-video understanding
Clear presentation with comprehensive statistics, well-designed figures, and logical organization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of ReferMo: primarily combines existing components (Swin Transformer, ReferDINO, SAM2, MPEG-4 motion vectors) without significant methodological innovation; motion encoding approach uses standard MPEG-4 technique

Questionable comparison fairness: ReferMo only performs language-guided reasoning on keyframes while using SAM2 for non-keyframe propagation, whereas baseline Transformer methods perform vision-language fusion on all frames—this architectural difference makes direct comparison problematic and unclear whether improvements stem from motion or from reduced supervision

Critical gap in analysis: Table 2 shows all methods achieve nearly identical tIoU (~68-72) despite 18-point J&F variance, suggesting temporal consistency is NOT the bottleneck—yet the paper emphasizes new temporal metrics. This undermines the motivation for tIoU and vIoU and leaves their utility questionable

Insufficient investigation of baseline failures: SAM2-based methods (VideoLISA, GLUS, SAMWISE) dramatically underperform (33-36 J&F), but only brief speculation is provided; no analysis of why methods designed for video tracking fail on this benchmark

Missing annotation quality metrics: no inter-annotator agreement scores, expertise level of 20 college annotators unclear, and no final quality statistics provided despite iterative check-correct workflow

Dataset composition bias inadequately addressed: heavily human-centric (71.9% humans, 12.7% animals, 15.4% instruments) with potential limited generalization to non-human domains; no discussion of limitations or mitigation strategies

Training setup raises fairness concerns: all baselines trained for only 6 epochs with hyperparameters following ReferDINO defaults—not optimized for individual methods; no exploration of whether longer training or tuning could improve baselines

Lacks comprehensive error analysis: no qualitative failure cases, no breakdown by challenge type (occlusion vs. disappearance vs. shot changes), no analysis of performance by object duration or description type difficulty
Limited cross-dataset validation: no comparison with LVOS benchmark mentioned in related work; no analysis of transfer from short-video to long-video datasets

Incomplete technical justification: motion at H/16×W/16 resolution impact on small objects unexplored; edge case handling in metric definitions (both empty predictions) not discussed; SAM2 version and exact mask generation settings not fully specified

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in RVOS: first minute-level benchmark for long-term video segmentation with 2,193 videos averaging 60+ seconds, vs. existing datasets limited to 1-15 seconds

High-quality dataset construction with rigorous annotation workflow: iterative check-correct cycles with SAM2-based refinement, expert validation, and no artificial text augmentation resulting in 24,689 authentic descriptions

Novel contribution of tIoU and vIoU metrics for temporal and spatiotemporal consistency evaluation, addressing overlooked limitation of frame-wise metrics in handling occlusion and object disappearance

Comprehensive benchmarking of 6 SOTA methods revealing critical finding: SAM2-based methods (SOTA on short videos) fail catastrophically on long videos, indicating gains stem from tracking rather than language understanding

Substantial dataset diversity: 163 object classes, multiple video sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), balanced description types (35% static, 32.5% dynamic, 32.45% hybrid), and oracle analysis showing 25% performance gap to MeViS
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement, comprehensive statistics, and systematic evaluation protocol that will facilitate future research
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in ReferMo baseline: uses standard MPEG-4 keyframe extraction, conventional self-attention motion encoder, and simple gating fusion (Eqs. 3-4); primarily relies on SAM2 for non-keyframe tracking without methodological innovation

Insufficient ablation studies: missing ablations on fusion mechanisms, attention components, clip decomposition architecture, and keyframe selection strategies; only motion presence/length ablated despite acknowledging multiple design choices

SAM2 dependency obscures contribution quantification: oracle SAM2 achieves 52.8-54.5 J&F vs. ReferMo's 52.8 J&F, making unclear whether improvements stem from proposed method or tracking quality; upper bound analysis shows diminishing returns

Incomplete analysis of long-video failure modes: no systematic ablation by video length, object duration, occlusion frequency, or disappearance-reappearance patterns; limited qualitative failure case analysis

Dataset quality concerns: mask annotations rely heavily on SAM2 (inheriting potential biases); no quantitative quality metrics or inter-annotator agreement reported; text descriptions from 20 college students without expertise verification

Evaluation metrics lack novelty and validation: tIoU/vIoU are straightforward extensions of standard temporal/volumetric IoU; no validation that metrics correlate with human perception or downstream task performance; no robustness analysis

Experimental limitations reduce confidence: only 6 training epochs with no learning curves; no cross-dataset evaluation (Long-RVOS↔MeViS); hyperparameters follow ReferDINO defaults without long-video justification; small validation set (113 videos) without confidence intervals

Significant data bias and incomplete analysis: 71.9% human objects limits generalization claims; no class-wise performance breakdown; no statistical significance testing on results; potential distribution shifts between source datasets unanalyzed
Reproducibility gaps: project URL not provided; SAM2 refinement details vague; no dataset/code release timeline stated; supplementary motion extraction details promised but unavailable

strengths: Addresses clear gap in RVOS research: first minute-level benchmark for long-term video object segmentation, scaling from 4-13s to 60+ seconds on average with 2,193 videos and diverse annotations

Comprehensive dataset contribution: 2.1M pixel-level masks, 163 object classes, 24,689 carefully curated descriptions with three explicit types (Static/Dynamic/Hybrid), and rigorous multi-stage annotation with quality verification
Introduces useful new evaluation metrics (tIoU, vIoU) that address real limitations of frame-wise metrics for temporal consistency assessment in long videos with disappearance-reappearance patterns

Thorough experimental evaluation: benchmarks 7 SOTA methods fairly, provides fine-grained analysis by description type, comprehensive ablations, oracle analysis showing 25% performance gap, and robustness studies across occlusion rates

Diverse dataset construction from multiple sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) ensuring variety in objects (163 classes), scenes (indoor/outdoor/egocentric), and description styles with balanced distribution
Clear demonstration that current SOTA methods significantly struggle in long-video scenarios, with comprehensive results showing method-dependent performance degradation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of baseline method: ReferMo combines existing techniques (MPEG-4 motion extraction from Video-LaVIT, standard spatial/channel gating, dual cross-attention, SAM2 tracking) without significant methodological innovation; local-to-global architecture is intuitive but not novel

Heavy dependence on SAM2: ReferMo only predicts keyframe masks while SAM2 provides temporal tracking; Table 4c shows SAM2 contributes 2.5-2.7 J&F (~5% of 52.9 total), making it difficult to isolate ReferMo's true contribution to long-video understanding

Concerningly low absolute performance raises questions about task formulation: ReferMo achieves 52.9 J&F overall vs. 80.6 J&F oracle on MeViS (shorter videos), with 25% gap between oracle and actual performance suggesting fundamental difficulty; very low vIoU scores (8-47) across all methods warrant investigation of metric design

Significant dataset bias not adequately mitigated: 71.9% human instances dominate; animals (12.7%) and instruments (15.4%) severely underrepresented; exclusion of background stuff classes mentioned only in supplementary material without justification, limiting generalization claims

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: paper shows models struggle but provides limited insight into root causes; large performance gap between Dynamic (49.3 J&F) vs. Static (55.8 J&F) descriptions unexplored; limited investigation of which long-video phenomena (long disappearances, view changes, occlusion sequences) are hardest

Dataset construction choices lack justification: >20 second threshold, 6-clip sampling, 3-frame motion vectors appear arbitrary without ablations or rationale; fair comparison concerns as existing methods trained on 4-8 frames but tested on all frames, while ReferMo trains on keyframes only

Evaluation metrics lack validation: tIoU remains 'relatively stable' across methods despite large J&F variation (suggesting possible lack of discriminative power); no discussion of metric correlation with perceptual quality; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Missing critical analyses: no inter-annotator agreement statistics for text annotations; no error mode analysis or qualitative failure cases; no annotation cost assessment; no discussion of practical applicability given low absolute performance levels; incomplete comparison to motion-focused MeViS (2023)
